title: Emergent aggregation from collective foraging
authors: Gorka Muñoz-Gil, Andrea López-Incera, Vide Ramsten, Giovanni Volpe, Thomas Müller, Hans J. Briegel
abstract: Collective behaviour in living systems is usually modelled as the outcome of a \emph{direct} social drive: agents are rewarded, or hard-wired, to align with or approach their neighbours. Here we show that aggregation can instead emerge from an \emph{indirect} objective. We let reinforcement learning foragers, initially performing a random walk, optimize their dynamics from a purely individual reward for finding replenishable targets, while perceiving only their conspecifics and never the targets themselves. As the visual range grows, the agents undergo a sharp crossover from an environment-tuned individual search to a scale-agnostic collective one, and this crossover coincides with the onset of spatial aggregation. Thus a collective phase arises as a by-product of optimal foraging, without any direct reward for grouping. A minimal analytical first-passage model reproduces the transition as a crossover between the two search strategies. Our results identify indirect, resource-driven reward as a generic route to emergent collective phenomena.
summary: This work demonstrates that collective spatial aggregation can emerge purely from optimizing an individual's search efficiency for local resources. By modeling foragers using reinforcement learning, the authors show that as the perception range increases, agents spontaneously adopt a collective strategy that leads to clustering, without any direct rule enforcing group cohesion.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether collective aggregation in foraging behavior can emerge from an indirect, resource-driven objective rather than requiring direct social rewards.
main_result: Aggregation arises spontaneously as a by-product of optimal individual foraging strategies when the visual range exceeds a critical threshold, demonstrating that indirect cues can drive collective phenomena.
method: The study uses reinforcement learning simulations and analytical modeling by comparing Mean First-Passage Times (MFPTs) for single-agent versus collective search strategies.
model_or_system: The model consists of independent reinforcement learning foragers moving in a 2D box, optimizing their movement based on a purely individual reward for finding replenishable targets while only perceiving conspecifics.
key_observables: Foraging efficiency ($\eta$), Clark–Evans aggregation index ($R$), and the learned agent policies ($\pi$) conditioned on visual state.
important_parameters: Visual range ($r_v$), target depletion time ($	au$), and the reactive length ($\ell$).
main_assumptions: The collective phase is shown to be a by-product of optimal foraging, not explicitly programmed; the crossover is identified as a sharp crossover, not a true thermodynamic phase transition.
figures_summary: Figures show the sharp jump in foraging efficiency ($\eta$) vs. $r_v$, the shift in learned policies from structured movement to random walking, and the mapping of the aggregation index ($R$) onto the parameter space.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the RL framework, showing the emergence of two distinct search strategies (single-agent vs. collective), analytically deriving the crossover point by equating MFPTs, and finally confirming the transition using finite-size scaling analysis.
why_interesting: The concept of emergent collective behavior driven by optimizing individual utility functions is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and pattern formation in complex systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Model. An agent (blue) moves by continue and turn actions and perceives conspecifics within a vision cone of half-width π/8 and range rv. Targets (green, radius r) are not visible to the agents. A tagged agent (red) has just collected a target and is visible as rewarded for a time τR; grey agents are non-rewarded.

FIG. 2. Foraging efficiency. Mean reward per step η versus visual range rv in the cooperative regime. (a) Fixed tag time τR = 9, several depletion times τ. (b) Fixed τ = 2, several tag times τR. Below a τ- and τR-dependent visual range the agents recover the blind single-agent efficiency (dashed lines); above it, η jumps and plateaus. Error bars: SEM over 4 runs of Na = 50 agents.

FIG. 3. Learned policies. Continuing probability of the learned policies π for the three visual states, in the compet- itive and cooperative scenarios, at τ = 4, τR = 9, Na = 50. Dashed lines in no agent state: single-agent (blind) policy. Dotted lines: initial policy. Error bars: standard deviation over 4 runs and Na agents (collective) and over 12000 agents (single).
FIG. 5. Role of the depletion rule. Clark–Evans index R over the (τR, rv) plane for the competitive and cooperative scenarios for Na = 25, τ = 2, and Nt = 100.

FIG. 4. Aggregation. Results for an environment with Na = 25, τR = 9 and the cooperative scenario. a) Spatial distribution of agents over the final 5000 steps of a 15000 step run with Nt = 100 with trained policies at parameter values marked by the corresponding symbols in c. Four exemplary agent trajectories are overlaid. b, c) Clark–Evans index R for two target densities Nt. Left panels: R over the (τ, rv) plane; dashed lines show Eq. (1) with ℓ= 5, 8, respectively. Right panels: line cuts over previous plots; error bars: standard de- viation over 4 runs and Na agents.
